title: HTTP Semantics
subtitle: The unified specification of HTTP semantics for all protocol versions
summary: RFC 9110 defines what HTTP messages mean, independent of how they are written on the wire: resources and their representations, the request methods, the status codes, header fields, content negotiation, and conditional requests. HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 all inherit these semantics, so a GET or a 404 means the same thing in each. It replaces RFCs 7231, 7232, 7233 and 7235 and the semantics parts of RFC 7230 (caching moved to RFC 9111).

eli5.summary: This is the dictionary of the web: what asking for a page, saving a page or getting a "not found" actually means, no matter which kind of pipe the words travel through.

tldr.problem: HTTP's meaning was tangled together with the text format of HTTP/1.1, and every new version risked redefining methods and status codes.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9110 separates semantics from syntax: it defines resources, representations, methods, status codes, header fields and conditional requests once, for every HTTP version.
tldr.outcome: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 share one meaning, and only the wire encoding differs between them.

facts.label: Methods defined
facts.value: GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, OPTIONS, TRACE

today: RFC 9110 is the reference every web server, browser, HTTP library and API gateway is measured against. Developers meet it daily through method choices, status codes, ETag and conditional request headers, and REST API design.

hero.subtitle: The unified specification of HTTP semantics for all protocol versions

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 9110 defines the semantics of HTTP that are shared across all versions of the protocol (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3). It replaces RFCs 7231 to 7233 and 7235 and the semantics portions of RFC 7230, providing a single authoritative reference.

By separating semantics from wire format, RFC 9110 makes it clear that GET, POST, 200 OK, and Content-Type mean the same thing regardless of whether the message travels over HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, or HTTP/3.
sections.eli5: The web has several ways of sending messages, like different kinds of envelopes. This document says what the words inside mean, so "please send me that page" means the same in every envelope.

sections.title: Resources
sections.content:
HTTP is a protocol for interacting with resources, which are identified by URIs:

Resource
Any information that can be named by a URI. A resource may be a document, an image, a service endpoint, or any abstract concept.
Representation
The current or intended state of a resource, encoded for transfer. A resource may have multiple representations (HTML, JSON, XML) selected via content negotiation.
URI
A Uniform Resource Identifier provides the address and name for a resource: https://example.com/api/items/42
sections.eli5: A resource is a thing with an address, like a photo or a web page. What you actually get back is a picture of it, which could be a web page or a data file.

sections.title: Methods
sections.content:
HTTP methods indicate the desired action to be performed on a resource:

GETRetrieve a representation of the target resource
HEADSame as GET but without the response body
POSTProcess the enclosed representation
PUTReplace the target resource
DELETERemove the target resource
OPTIONSDescribe communication options
CONNECTEstablish a tunnel to the server
TRACEPerform a message loop-back test along the path
Method
Safe
Idempotent
GET / HEAD
Yes
Yes
PUT / DELETE
No
Yes
POST
No
No
sections.eli5: Methods are the verbs of the web: look at this, save this, delete this. Some are safe to repeat, and some change things each time.

sections.title: Status Codes
sections.content:
HTTP status codes communicate the result of the server's attempt to satisfy the request:

200 OKThe request succeeded
201 CreatedA new resource was created
204 No ContentSuccessful but no body to return
301 Moved PermanentlyResource has a new permanent URI
304 Not ModifiedConditional request; cached version is current
400 Bad RequestMalformed request syntax
401 UnauthorizedAuthentication required
403 ForbiddenServer refuses to authorize the request
404 Not FoundResource not found
500 Internal Server ErrorUnexpected server error
sections.eli5: The server answers with a number. 200 means "here you go", 404 means "I can't find that", and 500 means "I broke".

sections.title: Content
sections.content:
HTTP messages carry content (previously called "payload") that represents the state of a resource:

Content-Type
Indicates the media type of the content: Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length
The size of the content in bytes. Gives the content length in bytes; senders usually include it when the length is known in advance.
Content-Encoding
Compression applied to the content: Content-Encoding: gzip. Applied before transfer encoding.
Content-Language
The natural language(s) of the intended audience: Content-Language: en-US
sections.eli5: Every message can carry a package, and labels on the outside say what kind it is, how big it is, whether it is squished and what language it is in.

sections.title: Conditional Requests
sections.content:
Conditional requests allow clients to make requests that only succeed if certain conditions are met, enabling efficient caching and safe concurrent updates:

If-MatchProceed only if the resource's ETag matches (for safe updates)
If-None-MatchProceed only if the resource's ETag does NOT match (for caching)
If-Modified-SinceProceed only if the resource changed after a given date
If-Unmodified-SinceProceed only if the resource has NOT changed since a date
ETagAn opaque validator for a specific version of a resource

ETags enable optimistic concurrency control: a client can PUT an update with If-Match to ensure it doesn't overwrite changes made by another client since the resource was last fetched.
sections.eli5: You say "only do this if the thing is still how I last saw it." If someone else changed it in the meantime, the server says no instead of overwriting their work.

messages.label: PUT /api/resource/42 · If-Match: "abc123"
messages.note: Content-Type: application/json. Applies only if the current ETag is "abc123".

messages.label: 200 OK · ETag: "def456"
messages.note: The update was applied and the resource has a new validator. A mismatch would return 412 Precondition Failed.

viz.caption: The same exchange written as HTTP/1.1 text

data.title: Conditional PUT
data.code:
PUT /api/resource/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 31
If-Match: "abc123"

{"id": 42, "status": "updated"}

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "def456"
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 31

{"id": 42, "status": "updated"}
